notes: Base building is funded: each month's O&M money now also repays 85% of the previous month's construction as military construction, so building and expanding FOBs no longer eats the budget
Support areas stand down on their own once the AO's FOBs have room: their companies move into the FOBs and the support area closes

Every company has a home base. The AO overview shows housing: how many companies live at its FOBs, how many are in the support area or outside, and free slots. When it is short you get a Companies without a FOB alert, with buttons to expand FOBs into camps or major bases (the brigade's own engineers can do it). Units whose base is gone are sent to a new one

Brigade combat teams now deploy as real brigades: a heavy or infantry BCT brings its brigade support battalion (two sustainment companies and a medical company) and special troops (engineers and intelligence); a Marine RCT brings a combat logistics battalion, shock trauma platoon and engineers. These companies are not combat units: they follow the brigade into its AO, keep its FOBs stocked from the nearest hub every day, treat its wounded and build its bases. Embedded support costs 40% less to run than stand-alone companies

Personnel counts the whole brigade: a heavy BCT is about 3,800 soldiers, an infantry BCT about 3,400, a Marine RCT about 3,600, so Forces now shows personnel in Iraq and Kuwait on the scale of the real war (130,000–170,000 from 2004 to 2008)

Funding follows history: Congress paid for that force every year. Monthly O&M now covers about all of the running cost at normal congressional support, supplemental requests pass more often, and every six months of the occupation a war supplemental covers operations

Indirect fire: mortar and rocket teams near your bases now shell them regularly where the insurgency is strong, causing killed and wounded inside the wire. C-RAM, counter-battery artillery, force protection, bunkers and hardened billets all reduce it
